\section{Why Self-Verification Fails}\label{sec:mechanistic}

The diagnostic cascade (\S\ref{sec:method}) identifies \textit{where} self-consistency fails; this section probes \textit{why} by testing whether models can self-verify at the entity level.
We evaluate three independent probes on Qwen2.5-7B fine-tuned on Few-NERD ($N{=}8$, seed 42; full results in Appendix~\ref{app:self_verification}).

\paragraph{Entity Self-Judgment (ESJ).}
For each extracted entity, we prompt the generating model: ``Is [\textit{entity}] a [\textit{type}] entity in this sentence?''
Entity-level AUROC is $0.512$---indistinguishable from chance---with P(yes$|$correct)${=}0.500$ and P(yes$|$incorrect)${=}0.500$.
ESJ-weighted construction degrades F1 to $0.711$ (vs.\ greedy $0.794$).

\paragraph{Multi-Round Self-Consistency (MRSC).}
Re-prompting on disputed entities (agreement ${<}0.6$) with focused verification yields P(yes) separation of $0.0006$ between gold and non-gold entities ($0.5003$ vs.\ $0.4997$).
MRSC best F1 ($0.763$) falls below greedy.

\paragraph{Latent Self-Consistency (LSC).}
Mean-pooled final-layer hidden states ($d{=}3584$) provide per-sample latent representations.
Centroid selection ($0.759$) underperforms greedy ($0.779$); latent entity confidence ($0.839$) marginally outperforms majority vote ($0.837$) without closing the oracle gap ($0.867$).

\paragraph{The asymmetry.}
Cross-sample frequency agreement achieves entity-level AUROC${=}0.868$---the only effective entity-level signal---while all three self-verification probes fail.
Models encode entity-level quality in output \textit{distributions} (which entities recur across samples) rather than in per-sample self-evaluation capacity (whether the model can judge its own extractions).
This asymmetry---strong distributional signal, absent introspective signal---explains why entity-level construction succeeds (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}) while selection based on self-judgment does not.

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Test-time compute scaling complements model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling}: repeated sampling with majority voting \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, brown2024monkeys}, and extended chain-of-thought \cite{muennighoff2025s1} produce large gains on reasoning and code generation.
4	These successes share a structural prerequisite: the output space admits either exact equivalence classes (multiple-choice, numeric answers) or execution-based verification (code).
5	Named entity recognition (NER) breaks both assumptions.
6	The output is a set of typed entities; two samples from the same input routinely extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and no external oracle can adjudicate correctness at test time.
7	Without equivalence classes, majority voting reduces to heuristic frequency counting; without a verifier, best-of-$N$ requires a reliable proxy signal.
8	This structural mismatch raises a concrete question: can self-consistency signals that estimate quality well for reasoning tasks also \textit{select} better outputs or \textit{construct} better entity sets for structured generation?
9	We investigate this question for NER and validate the core findings on SQL parsing, treating NER as a representative instance of the broader set-valued generation problem.
10	
11	The question has practical stakes beyond information extraction.
12	Hallucination detection methods such as SelfCheckGPT \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt} and FActScore \cite{min2023factscore} rely on cross-sample consistency to verify individual claims: if a model's outputs agree, the shared content is presumed factual.
13	This reasoning assumes entity-level self-verification works, that a model can reliably distinguish correct extractions from incorrect ones through self-judgment or re-prompting.
14	We show this assumption fails.
15	Three independent probes (entity self-judgment, multi-round re-prompting, latent-space aggregation) all yield chance-level or negative results for a fine-tuned 8B model on NER.
16	Recent work \cite{yao2026consistency} demonstrates that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy across benchmarks but does not diagnose \textit{when} or \textit{why} this correlation breaks down at the selection level.
17	Our diagnostic framework fills this gap: four failure modes (degeneracy, low agreement, false agreement, LP compression) explain why strong instance-level correlation coexists with negligible sample-level selection gain.
18	
19	We call this disparity the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
20	Five quality estimation (QE) signals achieve rank correlations up to $\rho{=}0.45$ and AUROC up to 0.82 with oracle F1, yet no signal outperforms greedy decoding on SciERC ($p{>}0.05$ for all comparisons).
21	Only log-probability (LP) achieves a positive selection gain, and only on Few-NERD ($+1.39$\,pp; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.019$, selection family $k{=}19$).
22	To test whether entity-level methods can close this gap, we evaluated seven approaches: entity self-judgment (ESJ), multi-round self-consistency (MRSC), latent-space aggregation (LSC), heterogeneous temperature sampling (Het-T), adaptive sampling budget (ASB), self-consistency distillation (SCD), and a supervised entity verifier.
23	All seven fail across three datasets and two model families.
24	ESJ achieves AUROC of 0.51 (indistinguishable from chance), while frequency-based agreement reaches 0.87.
25	MRSC produces $P(\text{yes})$ separation of 0.0006 between correct and incorrect entities.
26	The supervised verifier achieves entity-level AUC of 0.923 but translates to only $+0.30$\,pp F1, with negative cross-dataset transfer.
27	A hidden-state probe confirms that discriminative information exists in model representations but remains inaccessible through the prompt-based self-judgment interface.
28	
29	These findings rest on controlled experiments across four NER benchmarks (SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}), two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), a 4B ablation, and sample sizes $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 32\}$.
30	We extend to Qwen3-72B in the zero-shot regime to test whether the capability ceiling persists at larger scale.
31	Cross-task validation on Spider SQL parsing (GPT-5.5, $n{=}196$) confirms the diagnostic cascade: degeneracy reaches 87.2\%, and the F1 failure mode dominates.
32	Our prescriptive analysis identifies three escape routes that work precisely because they bypass entity-level self-verification: entity-level construction via majority vote ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$; $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC, $p{=}0.004$), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and LP-based selection restricted to low-degeneracy regimes.
33	
34	\begin{figure*}[t]
35	\centering
36	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
37	\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals estimate instance quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, so selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$) bypasses the bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
38	\label{fig:overview}
39	\end{figure*}
40	
41	Our contributions:
42	\begin{enumerate}
43	    \item \textbf{Diagnostic framework.}
44	    A four-stage cascade (QE $\to$ degeneracy $\to$ agreement fidelity $\to$ LP compression) that identifies where and why self-consistency fails for structured generation, cross-task validated on NER and SQL parsing (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
45	
46	    \item \textbf{Impossibility evidence.}
47	    Seven entity-level methods $\times$ three NER datasets $\times$ two model families all fail to close the correlation-selection gap, constituting systematic evidence for a capability ceiling in entity-level self-verification (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}, \S\ref{sec:adaptive}).
48	
49	    \item \textbf{Mechanistic explanation.}
50	    Hidden-state probing reveals that discriminative information exists in model representations (frequency agreement AUROC${=}0.87$) but the prompt-based self-judgment interface cannot access it (ESJ AUROC${=}0.51$), identifying an introspection limit rather than an information deficit (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}).
51	
52	    \item \textbf{Prescriptive escape routes.}
53	    Entity-level construction ($+1.02$\,--\,$1.40$\,pp), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and regime-specific LP selection ($+1.39$\,pp on Few-NERD) succeed because they bypass entity-level self-verification.
54	    A degeneracy decomposition $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1] = (1{-}D) \cdot G_{\text{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ yields a critical threshold $\theta_{\text{crit}}{=}0.70$ above which self-consistency cannot yield meaningful improvement (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}, \S\ref{sec:theory}).
55	\end{enumerate}

Our diagnostic framework fills this gap: four failure modes (degeneracy, low agreement, false agreement, LP compression) explain why strong instance-level correlation coexists with negligible sample-level selection gain.

We call this disparity the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Five quality estimation (QE) signals achieve rank correlations up to $\rho{=}0.45$ and AUROC up to 0.82 with oracle F1, yet no signal outperforms greedy decoding on SciERC ($p{>}0.05$ for all comparisons).
Only log-probability (LP) achieves a positive selection gain, and only on Few-NERD ($+1.39$\,pp; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.019$, selection family $k{=}19$).
To test whether entity-level methods can close this gap, we evaluated seven approaches: entity self-judgment (ESJ), multi-round self-consistency (MRSC), latent-space aggregation (LSC), heterogeneous temperature sampling (Het-T), adaptive sampling budget (ASB), self-consistency distillation (SCD), and a supervised entity verifier.
All seven fail across three datasets and two model families.
ESJ achieves AUROC of 0.51 (indistinguishable from chance), while frequency-based agreement reaches 0.87.
MRSC produces $P(\text{yes})$ separation of 0.0006 between correct and incorrect entities.
The supervised verifier achieves entity-level AUC of 0.923 but translates to only $+0.30$\,pp F1, with negative cross-dataset transfer.
A hidden-state probe confirms that discriminative information exists in model representations but remains inaccessible through the prompt-based self-judgment interface.

These findings rest on controlled experiments across four NER benchmarks (SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}), two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), a 4B ablation, and sample sizes $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 32\}$.

Our prescriptive analysis identifies three escape routes that work precisely because they bypass entity-level self-verification: entity-level construction via majority vote ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$; $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC, $p{=}0.004$), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and LP-based selection restricted to low-degeneracy regimes.

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals estimate instance quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, so selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$) bypasses the bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Diagnostic framework.}
    A four-stage cascade (QE $\to$ degeneracy $\to$ agreement fidelity $\to$ LP compression) that identifies where and why self-consistency fails for structured generation, cross-task validated on NER and SQL parsing (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).

    \item \textbf{Impossibility evidence.}

    \item \textbf{Mechanistic explanation.}

    \item \textbf{Prescriptive escape routes.}

\end{enumerate}

\begin{abstract}
Test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning and code generation, yet for structured information extraction (IE), where outputs are entity sets with partial overlap, a persistent gap separates quality estimation from sample selection.
We ask whether entity-level agreement signals can bridge this gap.
Across seven methods spanning self-judgment, self-refinement, latent consistency, heterogeneous verification, adaptive budgeting, distillation, and supervised classification, we find that no entity-level agreement signal reliably improves selection for named entity recognition (NER), relation extraction (RE), or Text-to-SQL.
The failure is systematic: all signals yield null or negative selection gains on four RE benchmarks and SQL parsing (87.2\% output degeneracy).
A temperature ablation reveals agreement becomes actively misleading under elevated sampling (conditional $\rho{=}{-}0.048$ on Few-NERD), and a mechanistic probe identifies a gap between hidden-state frequency agreement (area under the ROC curve [AUROC] 0.87) and prompt-based self-evaluation (AUROC 0.51), an introspection boundary that surface agreement cannot cross.
These negative results delineate where self-consistency (SC) does succeed for IE: through paths that bypass entity-level agreement.
Log-probability selection improves F1 by $+1.39$\,pp on Few-NERD (Holm-adjusted $p{=}0.019$), entity-level construction via weighted voting gains $+1.02$\textendash$1.40$\,pp, and cross-model ensembles add $+0.42$\,pp.
Each exploits sequence-level or cross-model signals rather than entity-level self-verification.
A degeneracy decomposition confirms SC gain vanishes once output degeneracy exceeds 70\%.
\end{abstract}

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Train linear and MLP probes on Few-NERD hidden states to predict sample quality.

Evaluates with 5-fold CV x 3 seeds. Computes Spearman rho, Selection F1,
and Gap Closure % relative to greedy/oracle baselines.

Input: hidden_states.pt, labels.pt, logprobs.pt, subsampled_instances.jsonl
Output: results_goldfiltered.json
"""

import json
import os
import warnings

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

DATA_DIR = "/root/autodl-tmp/struct_self_consist_ie/output/hidden_state_probe_fewnerd"
SAMPLES_PATH = os.path.join(DATA_DIR, "subsampled_instances.jsonl")

CV_FOLDS = 5
SEEDS = [42, 123, 456]

MLP_HIDDEN = [256, 64]
MLP_EPOCHS = 100
MLP_LR = 1e-3
MLP_DROPOUT = 0.1
MLP_BATCH = 256


def entity_set(ext):
    return {(e["start"], e["end"], e["type"]) for e in ext.get("entities", [])}


def compute_ner_f1(pred, gold):
    pred_set = entity_set(pred)
    gold_set = entity_set(gold)
    tp = len(pred_set & gold_set)
    if tp == 0:
        return 0.0
    p = tp / (tp + len(pred_set - gold_set))
    r = tp / (tp + len(gold_set - pred_set))
    return 2 * p * r / (p + r)

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

NER exhibits oracle scaling comparable to reasoning ($c{\approx}0.5$; \S\ref{sec:scaling}), but aggregation cannot close the gap: degeneracy (17.8--67.9\%), limited headroom, and LP-quality alignment ($\rho$ 0.043--0.667) constrain it.
Temperature disentangles these at $T{=}1.2$ (degeneracy 14.9\%, LP $\rho{=}0.225$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}).

\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms, with gains positive when degeneracy ${<}22$\% and absent when ${>}31$\% (all $p{<}0.01$; Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}). Under 72B few-shot, construction fails yet QE remains effective (SJ $\rho$ 0.29--0.44; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}).
Alternative strategies (DALS, MBR, DGS) and supervised mixtures fail to beat greedy (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}, \ref{app:supervised_combination}, \ref{app:when_selection_works}).

\paragraph{LP compression and calibration.}
LP compression connects to broader calibration challenges in fine-tuned LLMs \cite{kadavath2022language, xiong2024verbalized}: teacher-forcing training and constrained decoding compress the LP dynamic range, leaving within-instance variation insufficient for sample discrimination (median LP range 0.041 nats on SciERC; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
\citet{yun2025price} observe similar diversity collapse under structured output formats.
Potential remedies---per-token LP variance, calibration-aware scoring, or temperature-adjusted LP---remain untested for entity-level ranking.
Two per-sample alternatives could bypass the LP compression bottleneck: Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} derives confidence from consistency of token-level self-evaluation, while P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} elicits the model's own correctness probability.
Both produce per-sample scores without relying on sequence-level log-probabilities; whether they suffer similar compression under fine-tuning with constrained decoding is an open question.

3	\subsection{Entity Construction as MBR Decoding}\label{sec:mbr_theory}
4	
5	Following the MBR framework (Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_proof}), entity-level construction selects $\hat{y}_{\textup{MBR}} = \{e \in E_\cup : \hat{p}(e) > \alpha/(\alpha{+}1)\}$ under balanced set-overlap utility; $\alpha{=}1$ recovers the majority-vote threshold $\hat{p}(e) > \tfrac{1}{2}$ used throughout (Proposition~\ref{prop:construction_mbr}).
6	Signal-derived weights $w_i$ yield quality-weighted MBR: $\hat{p}_w(e) = \sum_{i} w_i \, \mathbf{1}[e {\in} y_i] / \sum_{i} w_i$.
7	Weighted MBR improves when $w_i$ correlates with $u(y_i, y^*)$ within instances; when this correlation is weak (LP on SciERC: $\rho{\approx}0.2$; few-shot: \S\ref{sec:scaling}), weighting degrades (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
8	
9	\subsection{Scaling and Inverse Scaling}\label{sec:scaling}
10	
11	Oracle F1 follows $F_1(N) = a - b \cdot N^{-c}$ ($R^2 > 0.999$; Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_scaling}): Few-NERD ($c{\approx}0.61$) scales comparably to reasoning tasks \cite{brown2024monkeys}, while SciERC converges more slowly ($c{\approx}0.35$).
12	The ceiling grows, but confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp---a persistent aggregation gap.
13	The gap persists across scales: LP $\rho$ drops without fine-tuning, structural signals generalize (Few-NERD VC $\rho{=}0.416$), and degeneracy is model-family-dependent rather than scale-dependent (Qwen2.5: $31.7$--$46.2$\% vs.\ Qwen3: $13.0$\% on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale}).
14	
15	\paragraph{Inverse scaling under adaptive thresholds.}
16	Across methods and configurations, increasing $N$ \textit{decreases} construction F1 in 40 of 58 observed transitions (paired bootstrap, $p{<}0.05$; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
17	The threshold $\theta$ controls the severity of the precision-recall trade-off: operating below $\theta{=}\tfrac{1}{2}$ amplifies precision degradation with $N$, while $\theta{\geq}\tfrac{1}{2}$ mitigates but does not eliminate the trade-off.

\section{Threshold Regime Analysis}\label{sec:theory_scaling}

\subsection{Entity Construction as MBR Decoding}\label{sec:mbr_theory}

Following the MBR framework (Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_proof}), entity-level construction selects $\hat{y}_{\textup{MBR}} = \{e \in E_\cup : \hat{p}(e) > \alpha/(\alpha{+}1)\}$ under balanced set-overlap utility; $\alpha{=}1$ recovers the majority-vote threshold $\hat{p}(e) > \tfrac{1}{2}$ used throughout (Proposition~\ref{prop:construction_mbr}).
Signal-derived weights $w_i$ yield quality-weighted MBR: $\hat{p}_w(e) = \sum_{i} w_i \, \mathbf{1}[e {\in} y_i] / \sum_{i} w_i$.
Weighted MBR improves when $w_i$ correlates with $u(y_i, y^*)$ within instances; when this correlation is weak (LP on SciERC: $\rho{\approx}0.2$; few-shot: \S\ref{sec:scaling}), weighting degrades (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).

\subsection{Scaling and Inverse Scaling}\label{sec:scaling}

Oracle F1 follows $F_1(N) = a - b \cdot N^{-c}$ ($R^2 > 0.999$; Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_scaling}): Few-NERD ($c{\approx}0.61$) scales comparably to reasoning tasks \cite{brown2024monkeys}, while SciERC converges more slowly ($c{\approx}0.35$).
The ceiling grows, but confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp---a persistent aggregation gap.
The gap persists across scales: LP $\rho$ drops without fine-tuning, structural signals generalize (Few-NERD VC $\rho{=}0.416$), and degeneracy is model-family-dependent rather than scale-dependent (Qwen2.5: $31.7$--$46.2$\% vs.\ Qwen3: $13.0$\% on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale}).

\paragraph{Inverse scaling under adaptive thresholds.}
Across methods and configurations, increasing $N$ \textit{decreases} construction F1 in 40 of 58 observed transitions (paired bootstrap, $p{<}0.05$; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
The threshold $\theta$ controls the severity of the precision-recall trade-off: operating below $\theta{=}\tfrac{1}{2}$ amplifies precision degradation with $N$, while $\theta{\geq}\tfrac{1}{2}$ mitigates but does not eliminate the trade-off.
Methods using $\theta{=}2/N$ are most affected ($-3.09$\,pp on Few-NERD at $N{=}8$, $-6.90$\,pp at $N{=}16$ vs.\ greedy), while majority vote ($\theta{=}\tfrac{1}{2}$) reduces the delta to $-0.87$\,pp and $-0.60$\,pp respectively---a severity reduction, not immunity (Table~\ref{tab:theta_sweep}).
Few-shot demonstrations improve QE (CoNLL SJ $\rho$ $.30{\to}.44$) but not construction (all n.s.; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}), confirming signal quality alone is insufficient when threshold or alignment is misspecified.

\subsection{Degeneracy Decomposition}\label{sec:theory}

\noindent\textbf{Degeneracy Decomposition.}\label{thm:degeneracy_bound}
For any aggregation method $A$: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1(A)] \leq (1 - D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}}$,
where $D$ is the degeneracy rate and $G_{\textup{nd}}$ the oracle gap on non-degenerate instances.
For signal-based methods with alignment $\alpha \in [0,1]$, this tightens to $(1{-}D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:bound_proof}).

\noindent With $G_{\textup{nd}}{\approx}14.8$\,pp and $\alpha{\approx}0.068$, the critical threshold is $\theta_{\textup{crit}}{=}0.70$: when $D{>}70$\%, SC gain falls below $0.3$\,pp.
Across 16 configurations, all gains respect the bound (ratio 3--12\%; Figure~\ref{fig:bound}); the bound is loose because $\alpha$---not $D$---is the bottleneck.
Tightening requires improving within-instance alignment, which neither signal combination (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) nor verifier-based construction (\S\ref{sec:verifier}) achieves.

The cross-dataset transfer results are concerning too — the AUROC drops to 0.56-0.67 on held-out domains, suggesting the learned patterns are quite specific to the training distribution rather than capturing something more general.

I need to be careful about the caveats though. The supervised MLP probe requires labels during training, so it doesn't actually contradict the self-consistency impossibility result. 13	
14	A LightGBM entity-level classifier (5 features: agreement count, LP, VC, SJ, FK) achieves AUC${=}0.923{\pm}0.002$ under out-of-fold evaluation, confirming that entity correctness is learnable from the available signals.

\section{Adaptive Methods}\label{sec:adaptive}

Since instance-level selection fails (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}), we present approaches that extract value from multi-sample generation beyond single-signal sample ranking.

\subsection{Cross-Model Self-Consistency}\label{sec:cross_model}

Diversity from stochastic sampling within a single model is limited by architecture-specific degeneracy (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
Mixing samples from architecturally distinct models---which produce complementary error patterns---can partially bypass this bottleneck.

In an exploratory extension combining 4 samples each from Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B (both fine-tuned on SciERC), LP-weighted entity construction yields $+0.42$\,pp over pure LLaMA sampling ($p{<}0.001$, 95\% CI $[0.27, 0.58]$; $N{=}8$ total), suggesting cross-architecture diversity can partially compensate for within-model degeneracy.

\subsection{Trained Verifiers: High Discrimination, Low Transfer}\label{sec:verifier}

A LightGBM entity-level classifier (5 features: agreement count, LP, VC, SJ, FK) achieves AUC${=}0.923{\pm}0.002$ under out-of-fold evaluation, confirming that entity correctness is learnable from the available signals.
Yet this discrimination translates poorly to F1: OOF construction yields only $+0.30$\,pp overall, with per-dataset gains of $+1.28$\,pp on SciERC, $+0.55$\,pp on CoNLL, and $+0.02$\,pp on Few-NERD.
The near-zero Few-NERD gain despite AUC${>}0.92$ reveals that frequency-based threshold construction (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}) already captures most of the verifier's signal; SciERC---with low degeneracy and diverse entity-level errors---is the exception where learned discrimination adds value beyond majority vote.
Cross-dataset transfer remains negative (B2-v2: $-0.76$\,pp; B2-v3: $-1.02$\,pp on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:verifier_transfer}), confirming dataset-specific feature mappings.
Even a trained discriminator with near-perfect entity classification cannot close the aggregation gap, indicating the bottleneck is structural rather than a matter of signal quality.
This motivates future work on approaches that generate training signal from the target distribution itself (e.g., distilling multi-sample consensus into single-pass predictions).

1	\section{Why Single-Signal Selection Fails}\label{sec:selection_gap}
2	
3	\paragraph{Definitional vs.\ empirical.}
4	We decompose the correlation-selection gap into two layers.
5	The first is structural: four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates from a given input (\S\ref{sec:formulation}), so they estimate quality across inputs but cannot rank candidates within an instance---selection failure is a design property, not an empirical finding.
6	The second layer is empirical and constitutes the core diagnostic: LP---the only per-sample signal---suffers compression under constrained decoding, with 60\% of SciERC instances showing within-instance LP range below 0.041 nats (Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}), effectively eliminating the variation needed for sample discrimination. Even where LP varies, selection gains depend on LP-quality alignment rather than degeneracy alone.
7	Cross-instance $\rho$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}) is attenuated by varying instance difficulty; within-instance $\rho$ directly measures whether LP discriminates candidates for a fixed input, making it the relevant predictor of selection success.
8	
9	\begin{table}[t]
10	\centering
11	\small
12	\caption{Best-of-$N$ selection (macro F1) on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, 2-seed mean${\pm}\sigma$). LP is per-sample; others use consensus-proximity. $^\dagger$One score per input.}
13	\label{tab:selection}
14	\begin{tabular}{lcc}
15	\toprule
16	Method & NER F1 & $p$ \\
17	\midrule
18	Oracle & $0.775 \pm 0.001$ & --- \\
19	Greedy ($T{=}0$) & $0.645 \pm 0.001$ & --- \\
20	\midrule
21	LP           & $\mathbf{0.647} \pm 0.005$ & .29 \\
22	SJ           & $0.646 \pm 0.002$ & .67 \\
23	FK           & $0.646 \pm 0.001$ & .79 \\
24	EM           & $0.637 \pm 0.001$ & n/a$^\dagger$ \\
25	VC           & $0.623 \pm 0.004$ & n/a$^\dagger$ \\
26	\midrule
27	Random       & $0.610 \pm 0.003$ & --- \\
28	\bottomrule
29	\end{tabular}
30	\end{table}
31	
32	\begin{figure}[t]
33	\centering
34	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_selection_gap}
35	\caption{Correlation-selection gap on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Bars: QE $\rho$; line: $\Delta$F1 vs.\ greedy (3-seed mean). Despite $\rho$ up to 0.38, no signal outperforms greedy ($p{>}0.05$). Dashed green: oracle ($+13.0$\,pp); dotted gray: random.}
36	\label{fig:selection_gap}
37	\end{figure}
38	
39	Despite $\rho$ up to 0.38, no signal outperforms greedy on SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}; Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}); the oracle reveals 13.0\,pp headroom, but LP achieves $+0.2$\,pp ($p{=}0.29$), below MDE (${\approx}$1.5\,pp; $n{=}529$).
40	The pattern holds across CoNLL and WNUT-17 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
41	Few-NERD provides the definitive contrast: LP achieves $+1.39$\,pp ($p{<}0.001$; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.019$, selection family $k{=}19$) at low degeneracy (13.0\% vs.\ 17.8--67.9\%), while structural signals still degrade (VC $-1.79$, SJ $-2.14$\,pp; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).
42	
43	\paragraph{Diagnostic cascade.}
44	We identify a cascade rather than independent factors:
45	(1)~instance degeneracy sets the ceiling on possible improvement (SciERC 17.8\%, CoNLL 61.7\%);
46	(2)~within non-degenerate instances, oracle headroom determines the opportunity (CoNLL ${\approx}4$\,pp vs.\ SciERC 13.0\,pp);
47	(3)~LP compression limits exploitation of that opportunity (Few-NERD within-instance $\rho{\approx}0.5$--$0.7$ vs.\ SciERC $\rho{\approx}0.26$).
48	We did not find evidence that degeneracy alone predicts LP gain across datasets ($\rho{=}0.052$, $n{=}23$, $p{=}0.81$; post-hoc power: 80\% power requires $n{\approx}85$ for $\rho{=}0.3$; Figure~\ref{fig:degeneracy_scatter}), though degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
49	The cascade stages interact rather than combining into a predictive model ($R^2{<}0$); each is supported by controlled ablations (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
50
